title: Python arq Reference
bottom_line: When you write, review or debug Python job-queue code with arq, Claude uses this reference to get the arq API right instead of guessing.

blocks.title: Two things Claude keeps in mind
blocks.text: Jobs run at least once, not exactly once, so Claude makes them idempotent.

In a FastAPI or aiohttp app, Claude calls `create_pool()` once at app startup, keeps it on the app state and calls `enqueue_job` from the handlers. The worker is a separate process (`arq tasks.WorkerSettings`) and is never started inside the web app.

sections.heading: One request, from your words to working retry code

before.label: You ask
before.text: "Add background job to my FastAPI app, retries failed webhook deliveries w/ backoff"

after.label: Claude delivers
after.text: A correct `WorkerSettings`, an `enqueue_job` call with the function name as a string, and `Retry(defer=ctx['job_try'] * 5)` backoff. No API guessing.

nodes.label: Client enqueues a job
nodes.note: Your app puts the job into Redis.

nodes.label: Worker runs it
nodes.note: A separate process started with the `arq` CLI runs the registered coroutines.

blocks.caption: arq has two halves: a client that enqueues jobs and a worker process that runs them.

sections.heading: The skill needs nothing; the code it writes needs Redis

cards.title: The skill itself
cards.text: No requirements, no arguments and no environment variables.

cards.title: The code it writes
cards.text: Python with `asyncio`, the `arq` package (version 0.28) and a Redis server for the queue.

blocks.caption: Installs arq. The current version is 0.28.0.

blocks.title: Where the code connects
blocks.text: The code connects to Redis on `localhost:6379` unless you pass your own settings, for example `RedisSettings.from_dsn(...)` with a URL from your own configuration.
